title: Daughters and sons
hook: He gives daughters to whom He wills, sons, or both, or none (42:49–50)

segments.voice: Yesterday: shura, consultation, set between prayer and giving. Your line was consult.

A man is told his wife has given birth to a girl. His face darkens. He hides from people, ashamed of the news, wondering whether to keep her or bury her in the dust. The Qur'an describes this scene from the Arabia it came down into, and it clearly wants the scene to end. Surah An-Nahl paints it; Surah At-Takwir says the buried girl will one day be asked for what sin she was killed. Against that background, listen to the order of the words in Surah Ash-Shura when it talks about children: who gets named first.

Verse forty-nine. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Pickthall: "He createth what He will." Then: He gives daughters to whomever He wills, and sons to whomever He wills. Daughters first. In a culture where a daughter's birth could darken a father's face, the Qur'an lists girls ahead of boys, as gifts. Some early scholars noticed this; one is reported to have said it's a blessing for a woman when her first child is a girl, because Allah began with daughters. Verse fifty continues: or He gives both, sons and daughters, and He makes whom He wills childless. He is Knowing, Able. Four possibilities: daughters, sons, both, or none, every one placed in Allah's hands. Teachers draw from this that none of them is a verdict on the parents. Not a reward for having sons. Not a punishment for having daughters, or no children at all. The Qur'an's stories and the Prophet's life bear it out. Ibrahim and Zakariyya were old when sons were given. 'A'isha, wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, had no children, and companions came to her with their questions. The Prophet himself had sons who died young, and it was through his daughter Fatima that his family continued. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim gives raising girls a special honor: whoever raises two daughters until they're grown, the Prophet said, will come on the Day of Resurrection with me like this, and he held two fingers together. The verse lists four gifts, and the hadith makes sure the first is never treated as the lesser.

Bring to mind the children around you, one by one: your own, if you have them, nieces and nephews, students, a friend's baby, the child you once were, and picture each face for a breath. If you pray, thank Allah for each one; if not, simply be grateful. And if there's an ache here, a child hoped for or lost, let it be part of the sitting too.
Hiba, gift, the sense behind Ash-Shura's yahab, Allah's giving of daughters, sons, both, or none, with daughters named first. Today's word.
Your line: each gift is his. Daughters, sons, both, or none, and none of it a verdict. That's day five hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims greet the birth of a child with thanks to Allah and often an 'aqiqah celebration for both girls and boys; the hadith on raising daughters is widely taught as an honor for parents of girls.

fork.setup: in a culture where some men grieved at a daughter's birth, the Qur'an lists the gifts of children. which does it name first?
fork.reveal: daughters, then sons, then both, then none: every one of them Allah's to give.

original.note: Arabic: He gives daughters to whom He wills; yahab is the verb of giving a gift (hiba).

trapdoor: what you thought: God decides whether you have kids.
what it means: daughters, sons, both or none are each Allah's gift, and daughters are named first.

what a scholar hears: yahab (from hiba, a free gift) governs inathan before dhukur in 42:49; tafsir records the remark about a firstborn daughter; Muslim 2631 honors raising daughters, against the background of 16:58–59 and 81:8–9.

chat.says: Does the Qur'an see sons as a bigger blessing than daughters?
options: No; Ash-Shura names daughters first, as gifts, then sons, both, or none.
Yes; sons are named first, since they carry on the family line.
It doesn't mention daughters; it speaks only of sons as gifts.
chat.meaning: Verse 49 names daughters before sons, as Allah's gifts; teachers say none of the four outcomes is a verdict on the parents.
